title: The Stairwell and the Count
passages:
Adeyemi dragged Voss across the grating, her boots drumming against the metal. "Don't you dare go dark on me," she said, hauling Voss's limp arm over her shoulder. The amber seam behind them had already closed on empty air, sealing the door bus shut. Senn's mist pooled on the deck plates, thin as wet paper, reaching toward the node chair base where the copper hummed. "I'm still here," Senn said from the vent, voice frayed. "I can short the purge if you get me back inside."

The slate hissed, ink bleeding: *Operator 23 pending. Senn.* Renner's voice, mild and awful out of the wet ink, said, "You gave each half and called it a win." Voss's eyes snapped open behind Adeyemi's grip, clear and not static at all. She stared at the count climbing backward on the slate: 007, 008, 009. "Unfile me," Voss said, voice cracked. "Before it hits zero."

Adeyemi reached the stairwell hatch and shoved it open. A maintenance figure stood silhouetted in the doorway, console glowing amber. "Welcome back," the synthetic voice boomed. "Count is reversing. You've bought minutes. One more step and the purge flips." The figure's smile was a glitch. "Operator 19. Operator 23. Choose."

Adeyemi set Voss down against the rail and reached for the override. "Not a choice," she said. "We take both." She jammed her access key into the console, but the hatch wouldn't budge until the slate stopped writing.

The console flashed red and spat her key back out, slick with something that wasn't oil. *Not yet,* the slate wrote, unbothered. *The hand that files must unfile.* "Wonderful," Adeyemi said. "The furniture has opinions now."

Voss laughed against the rail, a wet and awful sound. "It's not the furniture. It's Renner. He filed me. Only the filing hand reverses it." She rolled her head toward the mist crawling the deck. "And the filing hand is currently a puddle with a grudge."

Senn's voice came thin from the vent. "I can reach the cradle. Tip the busbar and I ride the copper up." A crackle of static. "It'll hurt. I don't have a body to hurt with, but I'm fairly sure it'll hurt."

"Do it," Adeyemi said, and kicked the busbar lever.

The mist gathered itself, no longer paper-thin, and poured toward the node chair base where the copper hummed. The count stuttered—009, 008—then held. Inside the chair something caught. The amber seam along the door bus glowed white and split with a sound like a struck bell. Senn was in. The chair took the shape of a person made of fog and current, and the purge froze at 008, trembling.

"Renner." Voss wasn't looking at the slate anymore. She was looking at the thing in the chair. "You filed Operator 23. Undo it. You always wanted it done *properly*, so do it properly."

The ink bled, gathered, and for one moment the slate showed a hand—Renner's, or the memory of one—reaching back down the page toward her name.

Then it wrote: *Operator 23. Filing reversed at the third mark. Awaiting the fourth.* The maintenance figure's glitching smile widened. "The count resumes when the hand withdraws. It has not withdrawn." And the ink kept moving.

The ink kept moving, and this time it wrote a name. The wet letters crawled up the slate in a black seam, spelling RENNER, then paused over the fourth mark. The maintenance figure's console threw a red error that looked like a face twisting. Its voice came from everywhere and nowhere, tinny with distress. "Fourth mark accepted. Filers must become filed."

Voss's hand was on the override before Adeyemi could stop her. "No," she said, to the slate, to the figure, to Renner. "Not you. You said you wanted proper. Proper hurt." The ink bled. Renner's voice came out wet and tired. "I did. I'm still doing it. Operator 23, filing reversed at the third mark. The fourth mark is me. I unfile myself, and the hand withdraws. That's the cost." Adeyemi yanked the busbar lever. The mist in the chair pressed against the amber seam, and the count held at 008. The fog-body turned toward the slate, head cocked. "Renner," it said, and the voice cracked into two tones, Adeyemi's underneath. "Withdraw." The slate wrote, *I withdraw.* The hand left the page. The ink died. The maintenance figure said, "Choice resolved," in a voice like a door locking. The hatch sealed with a clang. The count on the slate began again, slow at first, then fast: 008, 009, 010.

Voss made a sound like she was being strangled. Adeyemi grabbed her shoulders. "It's not over," she said. "The count's moving forward. That's the purge, not the unfile. You just armed it." The fog in the node chair reached up to the slate and pressed its mist-hand against the empty page. The amber seam glowed. Something on the other side of the slate pressed back.

Something on the other side of the slate pressed back. The mist-hand Senn had shaped hesitated against the wet surface, and the amber seam flared a wary red. A voice emerged from the chair's base, wet and layered: "You're not Renner. You're the knot." Voss stiffened. "Then who are you?" "I'm the count." The slate shuddered, ink veins spreading like cracks across its face. Adeyemi lunged for the busbar, but the lever snapped back, locked out. The count on the face jumped from 011 to 012 in a heartbeat. "It's accelerating," Voss gasped. "The purge isn't waiting." The fog-body in the chair curled its mist-fingers, trying to grip the slate's edge, but the page dissolved into wet smoke, and what came through was not a name but a pattern: a sequence of numbers, a date, a location written in thin black thread. Tether Auto, Sector 4, 0347. The slate went dead. The amber seam hissed and sealed. The count went quiet. Then, from the speakers above, a new voice: "Resumption confirmed. Purge sequence active." And the doors to the node room hissed open, revealing a corridor of white light that hadn't been there a moment ago.

The light didn't flicker. That was the first wrong thing—station light always flickered, some bad ballast three decks down, and this corridor glowed steady as a held breath. Adeyemi stepped to the threshold and the dead slate lit up behind her, 012, 011, throwing her shadow long across the plates.

"Boots back," Voss said, not moving from the chair. "You walk down there, you don't come back filed. That's how these things end."

"Everything here ends by not-coming-back." Adeyemi didn't turn. "You'd rather sit and watch the number hit zero with your friend melted into a chair?"

From the node cradle the fog-body spoke, and its two tones had settled into one—Senn's, mostly, Adeyemi's still ghosting underneath. "I can see down it. Copper runs under the plates straight into Sector 4. Give me a second, I'll ride it. Don't walk in blind."

"Then ride," Adeyemi said.

The mist thinned, poured off the chair's arms, and slid into the seam where the busbar met the floor. The amber glow chased it. For three marks nothing—010, 009—then Senn's voice came back thin and far, like it had traveled a long wire. "There's a room. Cradles. Hundreds of them, all dark. And a slate bigger than this one, and it's counting too. Same number. It's counting down to zero, and so are we, and it's the *same clock*."

Voss went very still. "Same clock means when it hits zero—"

"Both stop," Senn said. "Everything stops. That's not a purge, Voss. That's a shutdown." The count hit 008. "Adeyemi. Don't come down here yet. The big slate's got a name on it." A pause, the wire hissing. "It's got all our names."

Voss didn't wait for Senn's voice to trail off. "Renner's name is on that slate."

The words cracked across the white light like a gunshot, startling the silence that had settled over the node room. Adeyemi's hand found the busbar, knuckles white against the cold metal. "They withdrew. They unfiled themselves. How—"

"Someone put it back." Voss's voice was harder now, cynical in a way that suggested she'd known this possibility all along. "Someone who shouldn't be there."

The slate behind Adeyemi rippled. Ink bled toward the edges, dark veins spreading across the wet surface like something alive. The count dropped without their agreement—007, then 006—falling like a stone, accelerated by some unseen hand.

"Eight down, forty-eight to go." Adeyemi's voice was harder now. "Let's keep going. Who's next?"

She stepped into the corridor, the white light swallowing her boots. The door hissed shut behind her, isolating the node room from the pale glow. Behind her, the slate pulsed—005—and somewhere in the deep heart of the station, the copper hummed, its vibration traveling through the plates, waiting.

The white light didn't abate. If anything, it grew steadier, pressing against Adeyemi's retinas like an open wound. The busbar hummed through the plates, a frequency she could feel in her molars, and she quickened her pace, boots finding purchase on the smooth surface. Behind her, the node room door hissed shut with a sound like a held breath released, locking her into the corridor's long reach.

Further down, the cradles began to resolve from the glare—hundreds of dark shapes, some occupied, some not, each a name on a slate that mattered. Her own name sat among them, filed and waiting, but the count continued its merciless tick. 004. 003.

Up ahead, the white light opened into a chamber larger than any she'd seen on the node levels. The big slate stood there, impossible in its scale, bearing not just the five of them but every soul who'd ever filed a mark. And written in a hand that wasn't Renner's, in ink that bled cold, was a sixth name—slashed through, as if someone had tried to erase it but the slate refused to let go.

The count hit 002.

Something shifted in the copper below. A door slid open that hadn't been there before, revealing a staircase descending into darkness, and a voice came through the light, too quiet for the corridor but clear enough: "You're close now. The fourth mark unfiled herself. The count knows. What do you do?"

She looked down before she could stop herself. The amber wasn't ink from the slate anymore; it was gathering in the seams of the deck, thick as oil, and it moved against gravity toward the sixth name. Adeyemi put her palm back on the busbar, and the cold metal bit her hand hard enough to leave a mark. The white light above her went silent. Not dimmed—the source had closed its eye, like a mouth that had swallowed. The count on the big slate wasn't numbers anymore. It was a smear of white-hot ink, and through it she saw the sixth name whole, no slash, no burn, just a name written clean.

The station had stopped counting down and started counting the filing. The negatives weren't a countdown. They were a roll call. Each number it passed was a hand letting go. Adeyemi had let go. Senn had let go when she'd shaped mist to ride the copper. Voss had let go when she'd limped back to the chair. And the sixth name—the one slashed, the one Adeyemi had smoothed with her own palm—had let go hardest of all.

Behind her, the cradles began to hum. Not a sound. A pressure, low and building, in the floor. The hundreds of dark cradles shifted, and the dark shapes that had been occupied began to open their eyes. Senn's voice came through the copper, ragged and sharp: "Adeyemi, get out of the cradle chamber. The copper's not a stair anymore. It's a throat." But Adeyemi couldn't move. The amber had reached her wrist, warm as a pulse, and when she breathed it in it tasted like copper and old filings. The sixth name was whole. The rules said a slash meant burn. She had filed it, so the burn became a birth. And the station, which had been shutting down, was now waking up inside the filing.

The deck plates beneath her hands began to buckle, not with heat but with rhythm, as if the station had learned a heartbeat from the filing. The amber veins opened into fingers. They didn't reach for her. They reached for the busbar, and the busbar, cold and dead, began to warm around the fingers like a hand closing around a grip.

The busbar answered the grip. Its cold metal softened along the seam and closed around the amber fingers like a fist deciding to hold. Adeyemi felt the filing hand in her palm—the one that had smoothed AUTO whole—clench, and the roll call came back with it. The count stopped. 001. Then the big slate wrote a new line in her slant, because her hand was no longer only hers, and the line read: VOSS. The cradle across the chamber stamped her name in amber and slid open.

Voss stood in the dark mouth of it, not limping, not dead, wearing the limp like a coat she refused to take off. "You're late," she said, voice raw. "I was starting to think you'd let the station file me before you figured out you had a hand." Adeyemi couldn't answer. The amber fingers were still in the busbar, warm as a pulse, and the station's will was writing through her palm. Senn came coughing out of the copper behind her, blue mist streaming off, and said, "You stopped the count. Congratulations. Now you're the count."

The grip tightened. The busbar began to warm around the amber fingers again, not like a hand closing around a grip now, like a throat taking a swallow. Adeyemi looked down at her marked palm, at the white-hot smear still under her skin, and understood the roll call had not stopped being a roll call. It had just changed hands. Or names. Or wills. The slate's new ink in her hand was still wet, still her slant, still not hers, and it had chosen Voss. Behind them, the hundred cradles hummed the vowel again, and this time every dark shape that had opened its eyes was looking at Voss.

Voss didn't flinch. She looked at the cradles the way a night nurse looks at a ward that's about to riot. "Adeyemi," she said, voice raw but steady, "if you're going to write me, write me as the one who came back. Not the one the station shoved through the door."

The busbar throat clicked. The amber fingers curled, slow, like someone tasting a sentence. Adeyemi's marked palm throbbed in time with the deck plates buckling. The filing hand in her grip wanted to write again, wanted the next number, wanted the roll call to take Voss's letting go and turn it around. She could feel the station's will under her knuckles, bright and impatient, and underneath it—maybe—Voss's own stubborn pulse, the one she'd kept through the limp.

Adeyemi made her move. She didn't answer Voss. She let the filing hand write. The ink came out in a thin red line, then corrected itself, then wrote a word that wasn't a name: HOLD. The slate resisted, the glass warming under her palm, but the ink had come from Voss's palm, and Voss's palm had learned stubbornness. The busbar throat clicked again. The amber fingers around it tightened like a fist. The deck plates beneath her hands buckled in a new rhythm, faster, as if the station were laughing.

Voss's good hand lifted. The amber at Adeyemi's wrist flared toward Voss's palm instead of the slate, and Adeyemi's understanding landed hard: the writing in her hand wasn't coming from the station's will. It was coming from Voss's own palm, pushed through the filing, the way a body pushes air through a throat. Voss's let-go was still wet on the slate, and Voss had put it there. "Don't file me," Voss said. "You already wrote me. You just didn't mean to."

Adeyemi didn't let the filing hand write anything but HOLD. The word held on the slate, glowing faintly, and the busbar's grip around the amber fingers began to shake. Not closing. Not swallowing. Shaking. The deck plates stuttered, then went still. For one second, the station's will had nowhere to push. The silence was worse. Then the hundred cradles, which had been holding their breath in the dark, exhaled together, and every dark shape that had opened its eyes turned its gaze from the busbar to Adeyemi.

The exhales had weight. Each one came up through the deck plates and into Adeyemi's marked palm, and the filing arm quivered, wanting the next number, wanting Voss's wet letting go turned back into appetite. Adeyemi kept her hand on the slate. The word HOLD stayed there, glowing faintly, and the station's will—bright and impatient, hunting for somewhere to push—pressed against it and found nowhere clean. The busbar throat had gone still. The amber fingers around it had curled into a fist and stopped mid-close.

Voss's good hand stayed lifted. The amber at Adeyemi's wrist had already begun to drift toward Voss's palm instead of the slate, because Voss's palm was warm now, warm as a mouth, warm as the inside of a wrist. Adeyemi's marked palm throbbed in time with the filing arm's refusal. The hundred cradles breathed again, and this time the dark shapes turned their gaze from the busbar to Adeyemi—not away, not hungry, just attending. The hum settled into something that sounded almost like a countdown, or a name trying to remember itself.

Adeyemi made her decision. She let the filing hand hold. She did not squeeze the slate; she let the hand be held by her, grip and all, and the ink stayed on HOLD. The busbar's grip around the amber fingers shook, harder, and the deck plates beneath her hands buckled once, twice, then went still. Voss's lifted hand jerked—not toward the slate, but toward the limp Voss had worn like a coat. The amber flared after it, and Adeyemi's marked palm went white-hot under her skin. The real fight wasn't the hold anymore. It was Voss's grip on the limp, and whether the limp would hold.

Adeyemi stopped trying to out-stare the amber. She stepped into Voss's reach, caught the limp by its dead wrist, and pressed it back against Voss's side. The filing hand stayed flat on HOLD. Her marked palm screamed; her voice stayed level. "You want to carry it? Carry it without feeding it." Voss laughed, one cracked note. "You think I'm feeding it?" "I think it's chewing."

The amber slid off the busbar and wrapped Voss's knuckles, testing the warmer grip. Adeyemi felt the station's will lean after it, eager to file contact as consent, and she bore down on Voss's wrist—not pulling, just making the hold a refusal with a pulse in it. HOLD brightened on the slate. The busbar shuddered and spat a thread of copper smoke.

Voss looked afraid for the first time, and not of dying. "Let go of me, Adeyemi." "No." "You are handling me." "I'm holding you. There's a difference and you taught it to me." The cradles exhaled again, and this time the breath did not climb into Adeyemi's palm. It went to the limp. The dead fingers closed around Adeyemi's hand, patient as a latch.

The filing hand wrote nothing. The deck plates rang once, like a struck bell, and somewhere above them the sealed hatch unlocked.
